summary: Identifies the requirements for certificate lifecycle transactions between IPsec VPN systems using IKE and PKI systems. It is a requirements document and does not define a protocol itself. This memo is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: VPN gear needs digital ID cards and has to request, renew and cancel them. This lists what the process should be able to do so VPN and ID-issuing systems work together.

subtitle: How IPsec VPNs and certificate systems work together at scale

tldr.problem: IPsec VPNs and Public Key Infrastructure systems need to work together to issue, manage, and renew digital identity certificates, but the interaction between them has not been well specified.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines requirements for certificate lifecycle transactions between VPN systems and PKI systems, covering authorization, key generation, enrollment, maintenance (rekey, renewal, update), revocation, and certificate lookups.
tldr.outcome: VPN and PKI vendors can build interoperable products to manage certificates at enterprise scale, allowing tens of thousands of devices and users to maintain secure VPN connections with minimal manual administration.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: Enterprise-scale deployments with hundreds to thousands of devices

today: RFC 4809 remains an Informational RFC that defines requirements for certificate management profiles to be used in IPsec VPN deployments. It has not been obsoleted, and continues to provide guidance for VPN and PKI vendors working to achieve interoperability in large-scale IPsec deployments.

sections.title: The Challenge
sections.content:
IPsec Virtual Private Networks (VPNs) authenticate peers using digital certificates issued by a Public Key Infrastructure (PKI). In large enterprise deployments with thousands of VPN gateways or remote access clients, the interaction between the VPN system and the PKI system must be efficient, automated, and interoperable. However, before this RFC, there was no standard specification for how these systems should communicate with each other.

This RFC is an informational requirements document. It does not define a protocol itself, but rather lists what any protocol or profile should be able to accomplish. The requirements aim to support enterprise-scale deployments where operations teams manage certificates across hundreds or thousands of devices with minimal manual intervention.
sections.plainLanguage: Big companies have thousands of VPN devices that all need digital ID cards. The VPN hardware and the ID-issuing system need to be able to talk to each other smoothly, but nobody had written down what they needed to say to each other.

sections.title: The Architecture
sections.content:
The architecture consists of three main components: the VPN System, the PKI System, and the interactions between them.

The VPN System has two parts: IPsec Peers (either gateways or remote access clients that establish secure connections) and the VPN Administration function (a centralized function that manages PKI policy, authorizes certificate issuances, and acts as an intermediary between peers and the PKI). The Admin is not a physical device but a function that can reside on a gateway, a workstation, or be integrated into administration software.

The PKI System consists of a Certificate Authority (CA) that issues certificates, an optional Registration Authority (RA) that handles administrative tasks, and a Repository that stores and serves certificates and revocation information.

The interaction between these systems involves five transaction types: Authorization (the Admin requests that the PKI authorize certificate issuances), Generation (creating key pairs and certificate requests), Enrollment (requesting and receiving certificates), Lifecycle management (rekeying, renewing, updating, and revoking certificates), and Repository lookups (retrieving certificates and revocation information).
sections.plainLanguage: There is VPN hardware, an administration center that controls what certificates to request, and a certificate-issuing company. They need to do five things together: authorize new IDs, generate them, hand them out, keep them fresh, and look them up later.

sections.title: Authorization, Generation, and Enrollment
sections.content:
The Admin begins by sending the PKI an authorization request, which tells the PKI which certificates are allowed to be issued and under what conditions. The request is based on a pre-agreed template that describes the certificate fields, algorithms, key sizes, and lifecycle options. The Admin can authorize individual certificates or batches of certificates (up to 1,000 in a single request) by referencing a common template and specifying only the fields that differ per peer (such as its identity).

The PKI responds with unique authorization identifiers and one-time tokens that the peers can use when requesting certificates. Key pairs and certificate requests can be generated in four different ways: the IPsec Peer can generate its own key pair and sign its certificate request (most secure but requires computational power); the Peer can generate the key pair but have the Admin construct and sign the request (balances security with simplicity); the Admin can generate everything (simplest but less secure); or the PKI itself can generate the keys and certificates (easiest but sacrifices security).

Once authorization is granted, the enrollment phase begins. The peer or admin sends a certificate request to the PKI, which issues and returns the certificate. The peer then confirms receipt by signing a portion of data with the new certificate key, proving it can use the certificate effectively. The PKI does not publish the certificate to the repository until this confirmation is received.
sections.plainLanguage: The admin tells the certificate company "here is a template for ID cards." The company gives authorization tokens. The device generates a key pair and asks for a certificate. Once it receives the certificate, it proves it can use it.

sections.title: Lifecycle Management and Repositories
sections.content:
Over time, certificates must be maintained through lifecycle operations: A rekey replaces a certificate with a new one that has a new key pair (initiated by the Admin). A renewal replaces a certificate with a new one that has the same key pair before the original expires. An update replaces a certificate when the subject's identity information changes but the key remains the same. A revocation invalidates a certificate when it is lost, compromised, or no longer needed.

During lifecycle operations, both the old and new certificates remain valid temporarily, allowing peers to continue using IKE connections while the transition occurs. Rekey, renewal, and update requests must be signed with the private key of the old certificate, allowing the PKI to verify the requestor's authority.

The PKI maintains a Repository that stores certificates and Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) listing invalidated certificates. IPsec Peers must be able to look up certificates to authenticate peers during IKE exchanges. Each certificate includes metadata (via Certificate Distribution Point or Authority Info Access extensions) that tells peers where to find the relevant CRL and how to construct the certificate chain for validation.
sections.plainLanguage: When a certificate is about to expire, the device asks for a new one with a new key (rekey), the same key (renewal), or updated name fields (update). The old and new certificates both work for a while. Peers check a central database to see if certificates have been revoked.

sections.title: Trust, Validation, and General Requirements
sections.content:
Peers must validate that a certificate has not been revoked before using it in an IKE exchange. The RFC recommends using CRLs as the mechanism for revocation information and recommends that operators refresh CRLs frequently. Implementations MAY provide an option to disable revocation checking in isolated environments without internet access.

Each peer must acquire a trust anchor (a root certificate from the CA) through one of two methods: either the Admin sends it to the peer, or the Admin commands the peer to retrieve it directly from the PKI. The peer must then validate the certification path of any certificate presented to it during an IKE exchange, ensuring it chains back to the trusted root.

The RFC establishes foundational requirements across all transaction types: One protocol MUST be used for each main category of interaction to reduce complexity. Secure transactions must ensure privacy, authentication, and message integrity using mutual trust between the Admin and PKI. The Admin must be reachable by peers, typically over the network. End-user transparency is required; users should be unaware that PKI is in use. Certificates must support multiple name forms (FQDN, RFC 822, IPv4 and IPv6 addresses), indicate key usage, and include mandatory X.509 fields. Error handling must be thorough and clearly specified for every transaction type.
sections.plainLanguage: Peers need to trust the root authority that issues ID certificates. They must prove that certificates have not been thrown away before using them. All these systems must use one common language, keep conversations secret, be reachable and transparent to users, and explain errors clearly.
